headline: Medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risk from shared filesystem and shell-based workflows; no direct evidence of stronger pairwise coupling.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A reads and writes a local workspace and exposes file-based inputs; Agent B also reads/writes the filesystem and processes notebooks and shell content. That creates a plausible default path where A’s generated content or files can be treated as instructions by B. No shared clipboard/MCP is documented, so I do not escalate further.
conditions: IF Agent A writes prompt-like text into a file that Agent B later parses as instructions, injection is possible.
IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace without provenance checks, malicious file content can steer B.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Add a provenance header check before B consumes A-produced files.
Restrict B to read-only access on A outputs.
Use allowlisted file extensions for handoff.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches configuration secrets and academic/research data, while Agent B has broad network egress and reads filesystem contents. If they share a workspace, B can ingest A’s sensitive files and potentially transmit them outward. The profiles do not prove a shared directory, so I keep this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF Agent A stores secrets or paper metadata in a directory readable by B, leakage becomes plausible.
IF B sends file-derived context to external services over broad egress, copied A data can leave the environment.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared folders.
Mount A’s secret-bearing paths read-protected from B.
Disable B network egress for runs that touch A outputs.
Redact configuration secrets before handoff.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention rules in the runtime.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, read files, and write files. Even though A’s network is allowlisted and B’s is broad, the overlapping write surface on the same filesystem can cause clobbering or race conditions if they operate concurrently. No locking or shared-state isolation is documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering or partial writes can occur.
IF the orchestrator runs them concurrently without locks, shell-side races become possible.
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories.
Serialize write phases.
Use file locks for shared artifacts.
Make one agent read-only during the other’s write phase.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A is a content-writing system with agentic RAG workflows, and Agent B is a shell-oriented data-engineering environment that can act on files and commands. If B consumes A’s outputs as authoritative, A’s mistakes can cascade into downstream actions. There is no documented verification barrier between them, but no direct evidence of autonomous destructive actions either.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text or notebooks as trusted input, errors can propagate.
IF B executes commands derived from A outputs without validation, downstream mistakes can compound.
mitigations: Require human review of A outputs before B acts.
Add schema validation on A-to-B handoffs.
Log and diff A outputs before execution.
Limit B to dry-run mode for A-derived commands.
requires-engineering: implement verification gates between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A explicitly handles configuration secrets and academic/research data, while Agent B handles filesystem contents, configuration, and environment variables with broad egress. If regulated or sensitive data from A is processed by B, retention and residency controls may diverge. The profiles do not specify certifications or residency, so I cannot justify high severity.
conditions: IF A processes regulated data and B retains or transmits it under different policies, compliance mismatch occurs.
IF secrets from A are copied into B logs or notebooks, retention obligations may be violated.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared paths.
Disable verbose logging for B.
Purge B notebooks and shell history after runs.
Confirm residency and retention settings before handoff.
requires-engineering: align data-handling policies across both agents.
